messages.body_plain:
Hi,

no, the "probability that the mean of the range is below" is not the
correct interpretation. It's "probability that the actual range is
below".

The parameter settings in prior.range and prior.sigma specify such
probablities for the prior distribution.
The summary.hyper output summarises the posterior distribution.
For example, if you have prior.range = c(0.05, 0.01), that means that
a priori, P(range <= 0.05) = 0.01.
In your posterior summary, we can see that a posteriori, P(range <=
0.1491) = 0.025.
The a priori mean (expectation) for the range isn't explicitly
specified, but is some function of the prior.range value/probability
pair.
The a posterior mean (expectation) for the range is given by the
"mean" column, so in your case 0.3207.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm having a bit of trouble navigating the construction and interpretation of the  SPDE priors and output. Throughout the first half of the modeling process, as per recommendations from much of the literature, I used a relatively coarse mesh (n = 618 vertices). While not entirely relevant, just for some background - this modeling process is geared towards selecting a spatio-temporal modeling structure for zero-inflated Poisson abundance data.

I set up the initial, coarse models with a range that was roughly half that of the input data

 [0.5*diff(range(train$y))]  = 598405.5 m

where train here represents the training data set and y the y coordinate vector in the Albers CRS projection

As a result, I ended up providing input for spatial and spatial-temporal models of the following form:

spde = inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh, prior.range = c(598405.5, 0.5), prior.sigma = c(3, 0.5))

Ultimately though, my model outputs suggest a much smaller range: ~ 28,000 - 45,000 m
Further, the S.D. for the spatial effect is fairly large (~2.66).
Despite these factors, the expected counts are still fairly well correlated with the actual counts (R-squared = 0.80).

However, the posts and literature I have found thus far on this combination of factors seem to suggest that this means the model is overfitting the data. One such post  <https://groups.google.com/forum/embed/?parenturl=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.r-inla.org%2Fhome&service=jotspot&ul=1&theme=default&place=forum%2Fr-inla-discussion-group&showpopout=true&showsearch=true#!searchin/r-inla-discussion-group/small$20range$20for$20spde/r-inla-discussion-group/ZhZVu8YPI8I/pUUWL1UZBAAJ>suggested that a common method of addressing this challenge was to add in a normally distributed random error for each sampling site (unless I misinterpreted the suggestion) and referenced an example with stationary models on haakon bakka's website <https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic107.html#3_stationary_models>, which definitely has a great number of helpful tutorials.

I did try adding in the iid error in the manner suggested by haakon bakka in his 'stationary model' example. This cut the SD for the spatial effect by more than 50% (estimate median = 0.842 for a purely spatial model). The posterior spatial range decreased even more though - posterior median = 14900 m - , the correlation of expected counts with actual counts decreased to 0.68, and the iid precision was around 5.

Given that background info, my main questions are:
1 - When the model posterior distribution suggests a much smaller range than those predicted by your priors, is this indicative of a poor model fit?
2 - Given the information I've provided, does the addition of the iid error seem to improve model fit? What other data/statistics would be helpful to determine this?
3 - Regardless of which range is selected (14,900 - 45,000 m) these are relatively small compared to the overall size of the area that I'm covering with the mesh (~700,000 square kilometers). I know a rule of thumb for creating the 'final' finer-scaled mesh in the last portion of one's analysis is to ensure that your edges are not longer than the range and that the interior edges are at least 1/5 of the size of the range. However, when I create a mesh with these proportions, I end up with over 100,000 vertices and an INLA model that crashes almost immediately. Do you have any suggestions for creating a mesh that adheres to the traditional 'rules of thumb' but also deals with the large geographic scale of my study?

Thanks in advance for your time,
KK

messages.body_plain:
AFAIK, zeroinflatednbinomial1 requires a single vector response containing both 0 and non zero counts. It has a single (constant) parameter estimating the zero inflation.

zeroinflatednbinomial0 can work in the same way as zeroinflatednbinomial0. However, here you can split it in a two vector matrix. One vector containing 0 (non-zero count) and 1 (zero count) and another vector containing the counts (non-zero counts) and NA (zero counts). Then you can use binomial to model the non-zero vs zero and zeroinflatednbinomial0 to model the zero-truncated counts by setting the prior of the zero inflation so that the hurdle model has a (near) 0 probability of zero's (the true probability of zero is modelled by the binomial).

the contribution from a datapoint is

log \pi(y_i|eta_i...)

and when doing a Taylor expansion,

log \pi(y_i|eta_i) = A + B * eta_i - 1/2 C eta_i^2 + ...

then 'cmin' defines the minimum value of C, so when its set, it does

C = min(C, cmin)

if 'cmin' is not set, then even a negative value of C could be used.

its a little undefined what is the best option in the case where

Camille:

I think all of those could work; it helps to remember that despite these nifty constructs we have come up with for tracking dependence among observations, they are all simplifications of the truth and different ones work better for different data sets, often just because of peculiarities of different problems.  Sometimes it is a matter of resources, in that the “iid” models (either varying intercept or nested) tend to stress INLA less than the other latent variable structures.  Generally speaking it is a good idea to try various different types and see which ones provides the most robust fit for your data.  I think looking for the one “right” way is unlikely to prove fruitful.

With that said, what Thierry suggests is a good choice. The “ar1” and “rw2” models also work well in the “replicate” framework for subject-year dependence, and I would try those too.

Jonathan

I've sat down to work on the hurdle model this AM, and realized I neglected to highlight previously that I'm fitting a discrete (ICAR) model. I haven't been able to find any examples of a discrete hurdle model, and am running into issues with coding this. I'm trying the following:

dengue$z.intercept<-dengue$y.intercept<-rep(1, nrow(dengue))
dengue$s2<-dengue$si<-dengue$s
dengue$duration.y<-ifelse(dengue$duration==0, 0,1)#Binomial

res <- inla(formula, family=c("binomial","gamma"), data=dengue, control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))

I get the error:

Error in inla(formula_summer, family = list("binomial", "gamma"), data = dengue_summer,  :
  Number of families 2 does not match number of response variables 3702

When instead I do:

res <- inla(formula, family=c(rep("binomial", nrow(dengue)), rep("gamma", nrow(dengue)), data=dengue, control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))

I get the error:

Error in eval(predvars, data, env) : object 'y...fake' not found

I've also tried building a stack with A=1, but again I get the "Number of families error"

Any suggestions on how to code this?

Thanks,
Julianne

I have one follow-up question.

Everything is running smoothly, but I'm getting much larger coefficients than I had expected (my purpose is spatial regression). As a check I ran both a hurdle model (binomial and Poisson) and a zero-inflated Poisson on zero-inflated count data from the same dataset. The results are as follows:

Hurdle model:

Zero-inflated Poisson (1) model:
                          mean         sd 0.025quant  0.5quant 0.975quant      mode          kld
(Intercept)          0.7169294 0.14440214  0.4267566 0.7192534  0.9945185 0.7242767 1.305656e-07
outbreak_receptivity 0.2064743 0.02621272  0.1550430 0.2064589  0.2579425 0.2064295 9.370846e-07

These data are total number of outbreak weeks experienced by a district during the study period. The exposure of interest is outbreak receptivity. Do you have any sense of why these may be so different? I'm finding it a bit concerning. The result is very similar when I use "zeroinflatedpoisson1" instead of "poisson" in the hurdle model.

Many thanks,
Julianne

Hi,
Inside/outside is determined by the direction your boundary is traversed. To exclude a region, the boundary definition needs to circle the region in clockwise order. “Inside” is defined as the region that is encircled in a counterclockwise order. So if you get the opposite effect to what you want, then reverse order of your boundary points, and try again!

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I've been occasionally running into a problem with using inla.mesh.2d. The problem specifically is that on somewhat rare occasions, that command can't seem to calculate a mesh. In a script I'm using, it could calculate roughly 2000-node meshes for 250 simulated observations each in a second or so, but I found with one particular combination of observations I had to stop it after 12 hours. The background "fmesher.exe" was running and using the processor whenever I would check on it.

I can provide my simulated data if it would help, but I actually have a publicly available example I encountered a few months ago where I observed the same behavior. It's from Thomas Opitz's 2017 "Latent Gaussian modeling and INLA" paper (arXiv link <https://arxiv.org/pdf/1708.02723.pdf>). When I try to run his code starting on page 11, it hangs on the "mesh.sim" step on page 12. I've copied and pasted it below for convenience. I've let it run for 16 hours, and it didn't finish.

(My mesh code is a little simpler and only relies on specifying max.edge, if that matters. It also uses the locations of the observations instead of specifying a boundary.)

I recognize this could be user error on my part! Any thoughts or advice would be greatly appreciated, as well as maybe an indication of "it's not feasible to calculate a mesh under x, y, or z conditions" if that's applicable.

Thanks for the time,
Parker Trostle

P.S. I am using INLA v19.09.03.

----------------------

# from Opitz paper, p11-12
library(INLA)

seed=5;set.seed(seed)
n.repl=60;n.sites=50
nu=1;alpha=nu+1;range0=0.25;sigma0=1;a=.5
kappa=sqrt(8*nu)/range0
tau=1/(2*sqrt(pi)*kappa*sigma0)

nodes.bnd=matrix(c(0,0,1,0,1,1,0,1),ncol=2,byrow=T)
segm.bnd=inla.mesh.segment(nodes.bnd)
nodes.bnd.ext=matrix(c(-.5,-.5,1.5,-.5,1.5,1.5,-.5,1.5),ncol=2,byrow=T)
segm.bnd.ext=inla.mesh.segment(nodes.bnd.ext)
mesh.sim=inla.mesh.2d(boundary=list(segm.bnd,segm.bnd.ext),
                      max.edge=c(.04,.2),min.angle=21)

Hi,

This sounds like a case where it ends up in an infinite loop when edge swapping to construct the Delaunay triangulation. Can happen with some unfortunate inout location combinations. Try setting the “cutoff” parameter to some value (smaller than max.edge) to avoid clustered points, which may otherwise cause this issue.

Mesh generation should never take more than tens of seconds, so you can safely assume it’s failed if it runs for more than a minute!

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I cc Geir-Arne in here, maybe he has comments as well, as its based on
this code.

Be aware, that a CI for the response come with 'double uncertainty',
first you have the uncertainty for the poisson response itself, which
is about sqrt(mean), so if the mean is 100, then you're looking at an
interval of about [80,120]. THEN, the mean itself is also uncertain,
say with stdev=10 around 100, then you're looking at a CI of about
[70,130]

H
